content: Wood is a hard, fibrous, and lignified structural tissue that forms as secondary xylem in the stems of woody plants, including trees and shrubs. This tissue plays a dual role: it conducts water to the leaves and other growing parts of the plant, and it provides structural support, enabling plants to grow to significant sizes. The term wood can also refer to other plant materials with similar properties. Wood is a heterogeneous, hygroscopic, cellular, and anisotropic material. It is primarily composed of cellulose fibers (40–50%) and hemicellulose (15–25%), which are impregnated with lignin (15–30%). Humans have utilized wood for millennia for various purposes, including as fuel, and in the creation of artworks, furniture, tools, weapons, and construction materials. Historically, wood has been a critical material for building shelters, houses, and boats. Until the late 1800s, nearly all boats were constructed from wood, and it remains a common material in boat construction today. In many parts of the world, new homes are often built using timber-framed construction. Even in buildings made of other materials, wood is frequently used as a supporting material, particularly in roof construction, interior doors and frames, and exterior cladding. In North America, wood intended for construction is commonly referred to as lumber, while in other regions, lumber often refers to felled trees, and the term timber is used for sawn planks ready for use. Wood unsuitable for construction in its natural form can be mechanically broken down into fibers or chips, or chemically processed into cellulose, to create other building materials such as chipboard, engineered wood, hardboard, medium-density fiberboard (MDF), and oriented strand board (OSB). These wood derivatives are widely used in various applications, including paper production and as components of synthetic materials. Wood derivatives are also employed in flooring, such as laminate flooring, and in utensils like chopsticks, toothpicks, and wooden spoons. Formation A tree increases in diameter through the formation of new woody layers between the old wood and the inner bark. These layers envelop the entire stem, living branches, and roots. In regions with distinct seasons, this growth occurs in a discrete pattern, resulting in growth rings visible on the cross-section of a log. If the seasons are annual, these rings are referred to as annual rings. In areas without seasonal variation, growth rings may be indistinct or absent. Within a growth ring, two distinct parts may be observed: the inner portion, known as early wood or spring wood, is formed early in the growing season and is lighter and more open-textured. The outer portion, known as late wood or summer wood, is denser and darker, forming later in the season. In some species, such as white pines, the contrast between early and late wood is minimal, resulting in a uniform texture that is easy to work with. In contrast, hard pines exhibit a stark difference, with dense, dark late wood contrasting sharply with the soft, straw-colored early wood. In ring-porous woods, the large pores of the spring wood abut the denser tissue of the fall wood, creating well-defined growth rings. In diffuse-porous woods, the demarcation between rings is less distinct and may be nearly invisible to the naked eye. Knots Knots are imperfections in timber that reduce its strength but can be used for artistic purposes. In a longitudinally sawn plank, a knot appears as a roughly circular, solid piece of wood surrounded by parallel fibers. A knot represents a portion of a side branch or dormant bud included in the wood of the stem or larger branch. The fiber direction within a knot can differ by up to 90 degrees from the surrounding stem fibers, creating local cross-grain. Dead branches produce knots that are not attached and may fall out after the tree is sawn into boards. Knots are classified based on their form, size, soundness, and the firmness with which they are held in place. They affect the cracking (checking), warping, workability, and cleavability of timber. Knots weaken timber, particularly when subjected to forces perpendicular to the grain or tension. However, small knots located along the neutral plane of a beam can increase strength by preventing longitudinal shearing. Knots near the ends of a beam do not weaken it, and sound knots in the central portion of a beam are not serious defects. For applications where appearance is more important than strength, such as wall paneling, knots can add visual texture and interest. Heartwood and Sapwood Heartwood is the central, non-living wood of a tree that has become resistant to decay through genetically programmed processes. It appears as a discolored circle in cross-section and is usually darker than the surrounding sapwood. Heartwood forms with age and is not essential for the tree's survival, as evidenced by trees that thrive with completely decayed heartwood. Sapwood, on the other hand, is the living, outermost wood that conducts water and stores nutrients. Trees with rapid growth in open conditions have thicker sapwood than those growing in dense forests. The proportion of sapwood to heartwood varies among species and is influenced by the tree's growth conditions. Different Woods The properties of wood are closely related to the tree species from which it is derived. Wood density correlates with its mechanical properties, such as strength. For example, mahogany is a medium-density hardwood suitable for fine furniture, while balsa is lightweight and ideal for model building. Wood is classified as either softwood or hardwood, though these terms do not necessarily reflect the wood's hardness. Engineered wood products, such as plywood, are not considered raw wood. Color In species with distinct heartwood and sapwood, heartwood is typically darker due to deposits from growth processes. These deposits may enhance strength in some cases, such as resin-saturated heartwood in longleaf pine, which is resistant to decay and termites but highly flammable. Abnormal discoloration often indicates disease or injury, while fungal growth can produce attractive effects like spalting. Structure Softwoods, such as conifers, have a simpler structure with mostly tracheids and no vessels, making them more uniform. Hardwoods are more complex, with vessels that vary in size and distribution. Ring-porous woods, like oak and ash, have large vessels in the spring wood, while diffuse-porous woods, like maple and birch, have vessels scattered throughout the growth ring. Monocot Wood Some monocot plants, such as bamboo and palms, produce woody tissue that differs structurally and compositionally from dicot wood. Bamboo, in particular, is economically significant for flooring, panels, and veneer. Water Content Water in wood exists in three forms: within cell walls, in cell contents, and as free water in cavities. Air-dried wood retains 8–16% water in cell walls, while oven-dried wood retains minimal moisture. Drying increases wood strength, particularly in small specimens, with the greatest increase observed in ultimate crushing strength. Wood as Fuel Wood is widely used as fuel, especially in rural areas. Hardwood is preferred over softwood for its longer burn time and reduced smoke production. Wood stoves and fireplaces add warmth and ambiance to homes.
